query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A data-driven optimized thin-film deposition of nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy can create a robust, engineered passivating surface on stainless steel that significantly improves its corrosion resistance in extreme environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Stainless steel in its native state with a passive oxide layer that is ineffective under extreme corrosion conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface modification technique by depositing a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy film using deposition process parameters optimized through a data-driven/machine learning model.
generation.conditions: Extreme corrosion environments such as high-temperature molten salts or aggressive oxidizing conditions where conventional passivation fails.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, refined nanocrystalline passivating layer with protective phases on the stainless steel surface.
generation.mechanism: The optimized deposition process enables the formation of a strongly adherent, self-healing oxide layer that impedes corrosive attack by creating a robust diffusion barrier compared to the native oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: A marked reduction in corrosion rate and improved durability of the coated stainless steel relative to untreated material under extreme conditions.
generation.baseline: Stainless steel with its native oxide layer exposed to the same severe environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is constrained by the validity of the predictive model and the specific process parameter window; results may vary in conditions less aggressive than those tested.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by trends in advanced coating techniques, the exact quantitative benefit and optimal deposition parameters remain uncertain until further empirical calibration using the data-driven approach.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless steel samples: one set with the native oxide layer and a second set with the nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy coating applied using process parameters optimized via a data-driven model. Expose both sets to simulated extreme corrosion environments (e.g., high-temperature molten salts) under identical conditions.
measurements: Surface composition and passivation quality (e.g., via XPS or SKP)
Microstructural integrity of the coating (e.g., via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance, evidenced by comparable or higher corrosion rates, poorer passivation quality, or inferior microstructural/adhesion characteristics in the extreme environment compared to the uncoated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early work in corrosion resistance has shifted from merely relying on the native, passivating oxide layer of stainless steel to actively engineering the surface via deposition methods. For example, PMC7304825 demonstrated that nanocrystalline refractory high‐entropy alloy films deposited on stainless steel can confer improved mechanical and corrosion behavior by refining the microstructure and introducing protective phases. Although such coating techniques have successfully enhanced passivation and wear resistance, the selection and optimization of process parameters to yield consistently adherent, long‐term stable protective surfaces under extreme, aggressive environments remain a challenge.
decision.unsolved: There remains an open gap in reliably correlating processing variables (e.g., deposition conditions, annealing protocols) with resulting surface microstructures and ultimately with corrosion performance under extreme conditions. In other words, the complex interplay between coating formation, adhesion, and the development of a robust passivating layer is not yet fully controlled.
decision.lever: developing a predictive model that links surface modification process parameters (e.g., deposition energy, substrate temperature, annealing conditions) to the formation of optimal passivating layers and microstructural features
decision.why: A data‐driven approach would exploit accumulated experimental data from various deposition and post-treatment techniques to systematically optimize the surface modification process. This methodology addresses the complex, multi-variable nature of forming a protective surface and directly builds on the observed trend toward advanced coating methods, offering a pathway to tailor treatments specifically for extreme corrosion environments.
